name: Oak Ridge National Laboratory

profile.address: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Third Street, Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Oak Ridge, Roane County, East Tennessee, Tennessee
profile.reading: This facility at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Roane County, Tennessee, houses Frontier, a supercomputer operated by the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility on behalf of the United States Department of Energy. Oak Ridge National Laboratory is a Department of Energy national laboratory administered by UT-Battelle LLC, a partnership between the University of Tennessee and Battelle Memorial Institute, and its Leadership Computing Facility has hosted a succession of the world's fastest research computers since the 1990s, including the Intel Paragon in 1995, Jaguar in the mid to late 2000s, Titan starting in 2012, and Summit starting in 2018, each generation extending the laboratory's role at the leading edge of scientific supercomputing. Frontier, delivered in 2021 and opened for early science operations in 2022, is described by the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility as the world's first exascale system, meaning it is capable of executing more than one quintillion calculations per second, a threshold no publicly acknowledged computer had reliably sustained before it. The system is built on the HPE Cray EX architecture and uses the Slingshot interconnect for node to node communication, with 3rd Generation AMD EPYC CPUs paired with AMD Instinct MI250X GPUs, four accelerators to a node, spread across 74 cabinets on the machine room floor. Its storage subsystem was designed to deliver two to four times the performance and capacity of Summit's prior generation input output system, supporting the enormous datasets that exascale simulations generate. Frontier's peak theoretical performance is stated by the facility as 1.6 exaflops, and the machine has been used for research spanning fusion energy science, materials science, combustion and engine design, cosmology, nuclear reactor modeling and biological research, the kind of large scale physics based simulation and data analysis work that motivated the Department of Energy's decade long exascale computing push. As a federally funded national laboratory facility, Frontier's purpose is scientific and national research rather than commercial, and its capabilities are measured in supercomputing benchmarks such as floating point operations per second rather than the power capacity or square footage figures used to describe commercial colocation data centers. When Frontier was announced in May 2022, it topped the twice yearly TOP500 ranking of the world's fastest publicly benchmarked supercomputers, a list Oak Ridge machines have led before, with Jaguar and Titan each having held the number one position in earlier years, underscoring the laboratory's long running position at the front of open scientific supercomputing rather than a one time achievement.

reading:
Oak Ridge National Laboratory is a United States Department of Energy national laboratory managed by UT-Battelle, and the entry in this registry is its Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility, a DOE Office of Science user facility at One Bethel Valley Road in Oak Ridge, Tennessee. It belongs in a data centre registry because it is one of the largest single concentrations of computing in the country, but almost everything else about it differs from the operators around it. Time on these machines is allocated to researchers through federal programmes rather than leased, the siting and financing are federal rather than municipal, and the local planning, rezoning and utility record that anchors most pages in this registry simply does not exist in the same form.

What this registry actually stores is worth noting as a data quality point. The row is not a building footprint. It is a single mapped point named Frontier (supercomputer), tagged as a data centre with the laboratory as operator, and the location is recorded as Roane County rather than under the Oak Ridge mailing address the facility itself uses. The registry is holding a machine where it should be holding a hall.

Frontier is an HPE Cray EX system delivered in 2021 and opened for early operations in 2022, the first machine to pass one exaflop on the TOP500 Linpack benchmark. The facility's user guide describes 9,856 compute nodes in 77 Olympus cabinets at 128 nodes each. Every node carries one 64 core AMD Optimized 3rd Generation EPYC processor with 512 gigabytes of DDR4 and four AMD Instinct MI250X accelerators, each accelerator holding two graphics compute dies with 64 gigabytes of high bandwidth memory apiece. Nodes connect through four HPE Slingshot 200 gigabit interfaces for 800 gigabits of injection bandwidth and hold two 1.92 terabyte NVMe devices. The Orion Lustre file system presents a 679 petabyte usable namespace. The laboratory's own launch account describes roughly 90 miles of interconnect cable in the machine.

The power figure needs stating precisely. The TOP500 entry records 1,353.0 petaflops of Linpack performance against a 2,055.7 petaflop theoretical peak on 9,066,176 cores, drawing 24,607 kilowatts. That roughly 24.6 megawatts is measured system draw during the benchmark run. It is not a utility service rating for the building, not a standby generation figure, and not a critical IT capacity for the wider computing centre, which has not been published separately. At its debut Frontier also led the Green500 at 62.68 gigaflops per watt.

Its ranking history is a useful record of how quickly this field moves. Frontier held first place on the TOP500 from June 2022 through June 2024, second from November 2024 through November 2025, and third by June 2026, while its core count grew from 8,699,904 to 9,066,176 between the June and November 2024 lists. The facility also operates Summit, the IBM AC922 that debuted in June 2018, along with Andes, quantum resources through its Quantum Computing User Program, and testbed systems, and it has named two successors, Lux and Discovery.
